title: Gold Fell 6% in September. Can Diwali Demand Spark a Rebound?
excerpt: Surging Treasury yields and another expected Fed rate hike hammered gold in September. But cheaper prices are pulling Indian buyers back just as the festival season begins.
body:
• Spot gold fell more than 6% in September, touching $4,111 an ounce on September 28 — its lowest since August 5 — after a 13% surge in August took it to $4,386.
  • The trigger: the Fed's September rate hike and a spike in the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest since June 2007, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold; markets now price a roughly 70% chance of another hike in October.
  • For Indian buyers, the pullback is an opening: domestic prices fell to Rs 145,538 per 10 grams, the lowest in nearly two months, and dealer discounts narrowed from $43 to $14 an ounce as physical buying picked up ahead of Dhanteras (Nov 6) and Diwali (Nov 8).
  • Money managers' net long positions fell to their lowest since late July and gold ETFs saw modest outflows — but central-bank buying and the wedding season could cushion further downside.

Gold had a rough September. After one of the strongest monthly rallies in nearly three decades, the metal gave back more than 6% as surging bond yields and a hawkish Federal Reserve crushed demand for the non-yielding asset. The question for investors now: is the dip a buying opportunity — and will Diwali light the rebound?

What happened in September

The numbers are stark. The London Gold Price PM rose 13% in August to end the month at $4,386 an ounce, before the Fed's September rate hike and a spike in oil prices reversed the flow. Spot gold fell as much as 4% on September 28 alone to $4,111 an ounce, its lowest since August 5, as the 10-year Treasury yield touched its highest since June 2007.

"Today's fresh multi-decade highs in US borrowing costs have finally seen the gold price give way," said Adrian Ash, head of research at online bullion marketplace BullionVault, according to Reuters.

Positioning data shows the retreat is real, not just price noise. The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission reported that money managers' net long positions in gold fell to their lowest since late July, when bullion traded around $4,000 an ounce. Gold-backed ETFs recorded modest outflows of 1.6 metric tons last week, the World Gold Council said, though holdings remain substantial at 4,249 tons.

The demand side: China cools, India wakes up

Physical demand is the other half of the story, and it is splitting by geography. In China, the world's top consumer, demand softened ahead of the October 1–7 holiday, with local premiums over the global benchmark falling to zero.

India — the world's second-largest gold market — is moving the other way. Prices fell to Rs 145,538 per 10 grams this week, the lowest in nearly two months, and buyers are returning. Discounts offered by Indian dealers narrowed sharply, from $43 an ounce over official domestic prices the previous week to just $14, according to Reuters, a sign that the price correction is pulling physical demand back in. A Mumbai-based dealer at a private bank said jewelers and investors are showing greater interest, and gold could trade at a premium next week if prices stay stable.

That matters because of the calendar. India's festive season builds through Navratri (October 11) and peaks at Dhanteras (November 6) and Diwali (November 8), when buying gold is considered auspicious, before rolling into the winter wedding season. The World Gold Council, which describes the trade as "cautiously optimistic," noted that wedding-related buying has stayed "resilient" even as volatility left many consumers in "wait-and-see mode" after August's spike and September's sell-off.

"Despite the recent moderation, the trade remains cautiously optimistic about demand during the peak festive and wedding season."

— World Gold Council analysts

Investment demand: steady but shifting

Not all the buying is physical. Indian gold ETF inflows jumped 67% month-on-month to Rs 25.97 billion ($272 million) in August, pushing holdings up 1.6 tonnes to 121.3 tonnes, and digital gold purchases averaged Rs 25 billion ($262 million) a month from June to August — up 110% year-on-year.

What it means for your portfolio

For investors, the setup is a tug of war. On one side: multi-decade-high borrowing costs, the risk of another October Fed hike, and fading speculative length. On the other: central banks are still buying, physical premiums in India are tightening as festival demand approaches, and a stable dollar-gold range would confirm the correction is over. StoneX analyst Rhona O'Connell told Reuters that continued central-bank buying and stronger Indian demand ahead of Diwali and the wedding season could provide support.

The WGC's own bottom line is measured: it expects demand to improve into the festive and wedding season, "supported by steady investment demand and resilient wedding-related buying, though elevated prices and volatility may continue to constrain discretionary buying."

What to watch

Three catalysts in the next month: the Fed's October decision, where a second consecutive hike would pressure gold further; Indian physical premiums, which flipping back to a premium would confirm festival demand is real; and Dhanteras on November 6, the traditional peak buying day. If gold holds above $4,000 while Indian discounts keep narrowing, the September sell-off will look like a healthy reset — and the Diwali buyer will have called it right.

nri_angle: Indian festival demand is one of the few bullish offsets analysts see for gold in Q4; wedding-season buying has stayed resilient while Indian investors rotate steadily into gold ETFs and digital gold.
